sources.news_title: North Carolina GOP Picks State Lawmaker to Replace Rep. Chuck Edwards on November Ballot
sources.text:
North Carolina state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom will be the Republican nominee in the state’s 11th Congressional District, succeeding Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.).
The GOP executive committee in the district picked Balkcom on Aug. 10 as the GOP looks to keep the district and control of the House of Representatives. Balkcom will face farmer Jamie Ager in November. The Cook Political Report rates the district as “Lean Republican.”
The 11th Congressional District is located in Western North Carolina, where Balkcom was born and raised.
“It has been an incredible honor to fight for Henderson County in Raleigh, and I will take that fight to Washington and work every single day to make life more affordable for working families, improve community safety, support our farmers, and ensure we have the resources we need to continue to recover from Hurricane Helene,” Balkcom said in a statement.
In her statement, Balkcom lamented what she said is the Democratic Party moving further to the left with democratic socialists winning primaries nationwide.
“We must prevent that radical agenda from reaching our government, and that starts right here in the Eleventh District,” she said.
On Aug. 5, Edwards announced that he would drop his reelection bid following a House Ethics Committee report that determined he had acted inappropriately.
“After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign,” Edwards posted on X, adding that he will complete his current term.
The House Ethics Committee released the report two days prior saying Edwards should be censured by the House over alleged conduct toward two female staffers in his office.
The report accused Edwards of having “engaged in persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers.”
The committee did not find Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the staffers.
While Edwards “denied that any of his conduct was intended as a sexual or romantic advance, his pattern of behavior would lead a reasonable observer to interpret it as such, including providing the young women with lavish and recurrent gifts, making comments regarding their appearance and dress, inviting them to intimate dinners and vacations, sending notes regarding his effusive affection, and inviting them to other activities as a way to spend time together,” according to the report.
Edwards “was aware, however, that his excessive attention toward the young women had led to rumors and innuendo in the office,” the report said. “Both women were uncomfortable with his behavior (which they attempted to communicate) but were put in an untenable position by virtue of his status as their boss and a member of Congress. Rep. Edwards was at minimum blind to that reality, and at worst, dismissive of the impact his inappropriate conduct had on the careers and wellbeing of two women on his staff.”
Edwards’s office did not respond to a request for comment on the report.

sources.news_title: Balkcom accepts nomination to replace Edwards in 11th Congressional District race
sources.text:
RALEIGH — State Rep. Jennifer Balkcom (R-Henderson) accepted the nomination by Republicans in the state’s 11th Congressional District to replace U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) on the November ballot.
Edwards dropped out of his reelection bid in the early hours of Aug. 5, just two days after the House Ethics Committee recommended his censure over inappropriate interactions with two female staffers.
“I’m blessed to receive the Republican nomination for the 11th Congressional District,” Balkcom said in a statement. “Western North Carolina is where I was born, raised, and chose to raise my own family.”
Balkcom said it was an “honor to fight for Henderson County in Raleigh” and that she would take that fight to Washington, D.C.
“Like many Americans, the Democrat Party left me behind when they abandoned their values and embraced extremism,” Balkcom said. “We’re seeing that extremism play out across the country, as their party nominates radical socialists who want to raise taxes, open our borders, and do away with our way of life. We must prevent that radical agenda from reaching our government, and that starts right here in the Eleventh District.
“Rest assured, I will work every single day between now and Election Day to earn the votes of our friends and neighbors. Our region is incredibly strong and resilient, and I plan to be the fighter everyone who calls Western North Carolina home deserves.”
Balkcom, who was born in Henderson County and has remained there her entire life, has served as the District 117 representative for two terms after first winning the seat in 2022. She currently chairs the Committee on Insurance and the Appropriations, Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee, and she is vice chair of the House Select Committee on Helene Recovery and Appropriations Committee.
In addition to serving in the legislature, Balkcom has served as vice president of the Hendersonville Women’s Club and the Hendersonville Lions Club, as well as treasurer of the Mortgage Bankers Association of Western North Carolina. She has also held board positions on the Henderson County Education Foundation, the Advent Health Foundation Board and Henderson County’s Planning Board.
“Representative Jennifer Balkcom is exactly the kind of leader Western North Carolina needs fighting for us in Washington,” Merry Guy, Republican chair of the 11th Congressional District, said in a press release.
“She understands the people and communities of this district, and she is ready to stand up for our families, protect our values, and fight for the issues that matter most to Western North Carolina. Republicans across the 11th District are ready to unite behind her and get to work winning in November.”
North Carolina Republican Party Chairman Jason Simmons echoed Guy’s sentiments, stating Balkcom “has what it takes to be a strong voice for Western North Carolina in Washington.”
“She is committed to fighting for our families, defending our conservative values, and making sure Western North Carolina has a strong advocate in Congress,” Simmons said of Balkcom. “The NCGOP is proud to stand behind her, and we are ready to work together to deliver a Republican victory in November.”
Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.), who had urged Edwards to drop out, endorsed Balkcom in a statement on social media.
“Jennifer Balkcom fights every day for the people of WNC, whether it’s disaster recovery, supporting farmers, or standing up for women & girls,” Budd wrote. “I’m endorsing Jennifer because she’ll bring the values & strength of WNC to D.C., work to grow our economy, & always stand up for NC-11.”
Ahead of being selected for the seat, House Speaker Destin Hall (R-Granite Falls) praised Balkcom, calling her “the right person at the right time,” adding, “she will win in November.”
On Sunday, the day before the vote, Balkcom put her name into the mix for the nomination after state Sen. Tim Moffitt (R-Henderson) announced he was withdrawing his name, stating in part, “My responsibilities to my family and businesses would not allow me to commit to more than a few years in Congress.”
Adam Smith, the Green Beret who challenged Edwards in this year’s primary, also bowed out of contention. In a Facebook post, Smith said the seat “must stay in conservative hands” and that his decision was difficult, but he ultimately decided he needed to focus on his family and business.
“My family has sacrificed through my nearly seventeen years of service, the disaster relief effort after Hurricane Helene, and a campaign already this year,” Smith wrote. “My focus now is on them, on my businesses, and on the work I do every single day for this region.”
State Sen. Kevin Corbin (R-Macon) also turned down putting his name in. Other individuals whose names were floated included Matthew Burrill, who ran for the seat in the 2022 primary but lost; Ken McKim, who ran for state Senate in 2006 and briefly ran for Congress in 2021-22; Kristie Sluder, who ran unsuccessfully for Senate District 49 in 2024; and Chad Nesbitt, president of Skyline News based in Asheville.
Balkcom will have a sprint ahead of her against Democratic candidate Jamie Ager, who has raised more than $3.05 million, according to Federal Election Commission data from the period spanning July 31, 2025, to June 30, 2026. Edwards had not broken a million dollars for the same period.
Balkcom will have to start fresh in fundraising for her congressional bid with just over 80 days to go until the November election.
“Any money Jennifer Balkcom has raised for her state House campaign is essentially useless to her as a congressional candidate,” Western Carolina University professor of political science Chris Cooper told North State Journal. “Federal law precludes transfers from state to federal campaign accounts.”
The 11th District seat has shifted in partisan rankings in recent months.
The University of Virginia’s Center for Politics shifted the race from “leans Republican” to “likely Republican” this past May after the ethics investigation into Edwards was announced. Sabato’s Crystal Ball rankings moved the race to “toss-up” at the end of July. The Cook Political Report’s ranking has not been updated since June 18 and has the seat rated as +5 Republican.
The race for Balkcom’s current General Assembly seat will also need to be addressed by Republicans in District 117. Balkcom was facing Democrat Lynne Russo after winning in the March primary against Christopher Lamar Wilson with more than 76% of the vote.

In a statement following her nomination, Balkcom said Western North Carolina “needs a strong voice right now” as the region continues to recover from Hurricane Helene.

Balkcom won a competitive Republican primary in 2022 to represent the 117th District in the North Carolina House. She has also held several leadership roles in her community.
The 11th Congressional District includes a portion of Polk County and much of Western North Carolina.

sources.text:
North Carolina GOP chooses replacement candidate for Rep. Chuck Edwards on November ballot
North Carolina Republicans on Tuesday chose state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to replace Rep. Chuck Edwards on the ballot in November. Edwards dropped his reelection bid last week when the House Ethics Committee recommended censure.
Balkcom will face Democrat Jamie Ager in the fall. Ager won the primary in March, and although the district has not elected a Democrat since 2010, the party believes the rural, western North Carolina district could be competitive.
According to the North Carolina GOP, Balkcom won a competitive three-way primary in 2022 for her seat and is a lifelong resident of the district.
The change to the ballot comes less than 90 days before Election Day.
Edwards abandoned his reelection bid days after the House Ethics Committee recommended censure. It had concluded there is "substantial reason to believe" he violated House rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces.
The report said he "violated the House Code of Official Conduct by failing to adhere to the spirit of rules prohibiting sexual harassment of and unwanted advances to House staffers." It said it found that Edwards engaged in "persistent unprofessional and inappropriate conduct towards two young female staffers."
Edwards has denied any wrongdoing, which was also noted by the Ethics Committee report.
A statement on behalf of the Edwards campaign said the findings "completely exonerate Representative Edwards under the House rules governing sexual misconduct or harassment."
"They concluded that he neither engaged in sexual activity with nor explicitly propositioned any individual staff member. They concluded that the allegations in this matter do not implicate quid pro quo sexual harassment. They concluded he did not violate federal sexual harassment law," the statement said, adding that Edwards "looks forward to having his name cleared."
The allegations against Edwards come months after former Reps. Eric Swalwell and Tony Gonzales resigned after being accused of sexual misconduct. Meanwhile, the House Ethics Committee announced last week that it would investigate Rep. Max Miller, who is accused of domestic abuse and possible drug use. Miller had denied the domestic abuse allegations and said he had a prescription for drugs. The deadline for Republicans to replace him on the ballot has passed, and Miller has insisted he is staying in the race.

sources.news_title: Jennifer Balkcom Wins GOP Nomination in North Carolina’s 11th District
sources.text:
North Carolina state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom has won the Republican nomination for the state’s 11th Congressional District, setting up a general election contest against Democrat Jamie Ager after incumbent Rep. Chuck Edwards ended his reelection campaign amid a House Ethics Committee investigation.
Balkcom was selected Monday evening by the 11th Congressional District Republican Executive Committee, a group of local Republican Party members that includes county party leaders. Republicans were tasked with choosing a new nominee after Edwards withdrew from the race last week.
The National Republican Congressional Committee congratulated Balkcom following her selection, saying she would “deliver results for Western North Carolina by strengthening the economy, supporting farmers & securing the border.”
Balkcom, who currently serves in the North Carolina State House, announced before her selection that she was seeking the nomination after receiving encouragement to run.
“For eight generations, my family has called Western North Carolina home,” Balkcom said in a statement. “My roots run deep in these mountains, and the people, values, and way of life here are woven into every part of who I am.”
Balkcom said she had not originally planned to go to Washington but ultimately decided to enter the race.
“Our communities are still rebuilding from Hurricane Helene,” she said. “Our farmers, families, and small businesses need someone who understands them. And too often, Washington simply doesn’t understand the people, values, and challenges of our mountains.”
She said Republicans need to hold the seat, continue working with President Donald Trump’s administration on rebuilding Western North Carolina, and ensure that Washington does not forget the residents of the region.
Balkcom described herself as a “Henderson County farm girl” and said those roots are why she fights so hard for Western North Carolina.
“Western North Carolina is worth fighting for, and I’m ready to get to work,” Balkcom said.
She will face Ager in a district Trump carried by ten points in 2024. Former Biden Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg endorsed Ager and traveled to the district to campaign with him. Ager is also endorsed by Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA).
RNC Research highlighted Ager saying that “immigration has benefitted this country in so many ways,” adding that for people who “have been here for 20 years” and still lack legal status, policymakers should look at “finding some way for pathway to citizenship for those folks.”
Edwards announced August 5 that he was ending his reelection campaign following the House Ethics Committee investigation while finishing his current term, writing, “After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign.” The committee said it found no evidence that Edwards engaged in sexual activity with or propositioned staffers but identified a “pattern of behavior” that could reasonably be interpreted that way, including lavish and recurring gifts, comments about young female employees’ appearance and clothing, and invitations to dinners and vacations. Edwards denied wrongdoing and disagreed with the findings.
According to an Axios report, Edwards gave two young female staffers personalized handguns, including a blue gun engraved with one employee’s name and a pink gun given to another, whose lawyer said she accepted it out of fear of employment repercussions before later legally disposing of it. Edwards defended the gifts, citing his firearms experience.
Axios also reported that he arranged a surprise performance of one staffer’s favorite Ed Sheeran songs at her birthday party, gave employees personal gifts including jewelry, a custom Adam Sandler puzzle, and a purse, held frequent one-on-one dinners with aides, complimented their appearance, and wrote one departing staffer a three-page letter calling her “the most amazing woman” and saying she had “written a complex chapter in my heart.” The outlet further reported that Edwards and a former staffer vacationed in Las Vegas months after she left his office and that his office had a 59 percent staff turnover rate in 2025, compared with a 27 percent House average.
NOTUS separately reported that the Ethics Committee was examining allegations that Edwards had an affair with a former deputy chief of staff whom he first hired while serving as a state senator in 2021, with sources saying the alleged relationship became widely known among staff and members of North Carolina’s congressional delegation and contributed to internal tensions and departures. Edwards welcomed the investigation while arguing that people with political agendas were using “false accusations” to generate news coverage. He was first elected to Congress in 2022 after defeating then-Rep. Madison Cawthorn in the Republican primary and previously served in the North Carolina General Assembly.

sources.news_title: GOP rallies behind last-minute ballot replacement for Congressman Edwards
sources.text:
The newly selected GOP candidate for Congress, Jennifer Balkcom (center), is pictured with the Haywood County delegation who served on the party’s selection committee: Joshua Mashburn, Kim Genova and Sherry Lewis.
The ballot for the Congressional west representing WNC is now set: Democrat Jamie Ager versus Republican Jennifer Balkcom.
The newly selected GOP candidate for Congress, Jennifer Balkcom (center), is pictured with the Haywood County delegation who served on the party’s selection committee: Joshua Mashburn, Kim Genova and Sherry Lewis.
Jamie Ager, Democrat candidate for Congress, on his fourth-generation farm Hickory Nut Gap in Fairview.
An 11th-hour name floated to take GOP Congressman Chuck Edwards’ place on the ballot garnered quick and wide-spread backing among the party — handily besting the rest of the field in a vote among WNC party officials Monday night.
N.C. House Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, R-Henderson County, was selected as the GOP choice to run for Edwards’ seat. Edwards abruptly departed from the race last week amid a sexual harassment scandal involving two young female staffers.
The GOP was in a frenzy to select a last-minute candidate in short order so ballots could finalized by next week. And the stakes were high. The candidate would be facing-off against Democrat Jamie Ager who was not only polling neck-in-neck with Edwards, but also out fundraising him three-to-one.
Party representives from across the 16-county Congressional district gathered at Buncombe County GOP headquarters Monday evening to select Edwards’ replacement in the race. There were six candidates in all.
“Each candidate got six minutes to speak. After all six spoke, we voted. And it was decided in one round,” said Kim Genova, chair of the Haywood County GOP.
The winning candidate had to secure more than 50% of the vote — at least 27 out of the 51 party officials tasked with making the decision. If none of the six passed muster on the first round, the slate would be narrowed before going to a second round of voting, and so forth.
But Balkcom secured the needed votes out of the gate. Genova said Balkcom is exactly who the party needs, witnessed by the overwhelming support she garnered.
“This was a unique situation, and people took it seriously,” Genova said. “We all feel really good about this, and I am so excited to campaign for her.”
Balkcom was a late contender after N.C. Sen. Tim Moffitt — a presumptive favorite in the days leading up to the party vote — announced Sunday he wouldn’t put his name in the hat after all. Balkcom, who’d planned to support Moffitt, then entered the ring herself, calling the race “too important to sit out.”
“It was a moving target all weekend as to who would be on the ballot,” Genova said. “I was waiting for her name to drop, and when it did, I had a huge sigh of relief that ‘We can win this.’”
She’ll face stout competition from Ager. He has a family pedigree in WNC politics and is a fourth-generation farmer from Fairview with Hickory Nut Gap Farm. While Balkcom’s career has been in mortgage banking, she grew up on a family farm, and was quick to try to move in on Ager’s brand as a farmer.
“I’m a Henderson County farm girl. I know what it means to work hard, fight for what you believe in and protect something so the next generation can inherit it,” she said.
Despite the stain of Edwards’ ethics investigation, the party is determined to look foward, not backward, said Joshua Mashburn, a member of the Haywood County GOP executive committee who was on the selection panel.
“The executive committe decided we would all back whoever the nominee is because we cannot lose this seat — and we aren’t going to,” Mashburn said.
“We are hitting the ground running to get her elected in November,” Genova added.
Ager has a jump on Balkcom, however, having been on the campaign trail for nearly a year already. He’s raised over $3 million and had $2.1 million cash on hand at the end of June — compared to Edwards’ $1 million raised with $485,000 cash on hand.
Ager comes from a politically-connected family. His grandfather was a Congressman, his father is a former state legislator, and his brother is currently a state legislator.
“No matter who we face in November, I’m confident we can win this race,” Ager maintained.
But Balkcom isn’t daunted.
“Rest assured, I will work every single day between now and Election Day to earn the votes of our friends and neighbors,” Balkcom said.
Balkcom is currently serving her fourth year in the N.C. House of Representatives. Balkcom also used to be a Democrat before switching parties a decade ago.
“The Democrat Party left me behind when they abandoned their values and embraced extremism,” said Balkcom. She was briefly registered as a Liberatarian from 2002-2005, then a Democrat from 2005-2016.
The GOP will now have to select a replacement to run in Balkcom’s place in the N.C. House of Representatives race.

sources.news_title: GOP picks Balkcom to run in place of Edwards for NC congressional seat
sources.text:
A committee of Republicans in North Carolina’s westernmost congressional district have chosen State Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, R-Henderson, to replace US Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-Hendersonville, in the race to defend his seat against Buncombe County farmer Jamie Ager, the Democratic nominee.
Balkcom, who has served two terms in the state House, has less than 100 days until Election Day to campaign to keep the 11th District in Republican hands after the disgraced Edwards dropped his reelection bid because of misconduct with former staffers. She currently represents part of Henderson County in the legislature, and her seat in the House will be filled while she campaigns this fall.
“This race is too important to sit out,” Balkcom said in a statement. “We must hold this seat, preserve our mountain values, work with President Trump’s Administration to continue rebuilding Western North Carolina, and make sure Washington never forgets the people who call these mountains home.”
[Subscribe for FREE to Carolina Public Press’ Daily, Weekend and Election 2026 newsletters.]
Balkcom, who is herself from a farming family in Henderson County, will run against Ager who has been campaigning for the past year. The race has already been contentious, with debates between Democrat Ager and former candidate Edwards focused on long-term Helene recovery and holding FEMA accountable.
With a new candidate, whether the seat remains red or flips blue becomes even less clear. So far, Ager had significantly out-fundraised Edwards, but the seat has been held by Republicans since 2013.
Choosing Balkcom
The Executive Committee for the Republican Party in NC-11 had an emergency meeting Monday in Asheville to decide who would replace Rep. Edwards in the congressional race for the district.
At the meeting, which took place at the Buncombe County Republican Party headquarters and was closed to the press, committee members made nominations and voted on them until more than half of the committee decided on Balkcom. She was one of six Republicans seeking the seat.
The committee consists of 63 individuals who are county party chairs, vice chairs and at-large members. Earlier Monday, NC House Speaker Destin Hall, R-Caldwell, endorsed Balkcom in a social media post. Balkcom announced that she would be seeking the spot in the race late Sunday.
“We’re excited about the race and we know that she is going to represent this district well,” Merry Guy, the chair of the 11th District’s Republican committee, said after the meeting. She also said it would be her “full-time job” from now until November to get Balkcom elected.
Edwards leaves the race
Last Wednesday, Edwards announced his decision to drop his reelection bid for the 11th Congressional District, which came days after the House Ethics Committee recommended censuring him for inappropriate behavior toward two young, female staffers. Investigators found that Edwards gave the two staffers expensive gifts and vacations, took them on one-on-one dinners and skipped votes to help one decorate her Christmas tree. Both staffers resigned after rumors of their relationship with Edwards became public.
In a post on the social media site X, Edwards said that he will finish out his term. He has represented the 11th District in Congress since 2022, winning the Republican primary against the controversial former representative Madison Cawthorn.
A number of other nominees were in the running but Balkcom won on the first vote, according to Zach Almond, the director of the North Carolina Republican Party.
Other Republicans in Western North Carolina made statements this past week that they would not be seeking Edwards’ spot in the race. State Sen. Kevin Corbin, R-Macon, issued a statement last week after Edwards announced his decision to not pursue Edwards’ seat for a myriad of reasons, one being his position on a Hurricane Helene recovery committee.
State Sen. Tim Moffitt, R-Henderson, and Adam Smith, an Army veteran who ran against Edwards in the Republican primary earlier this year, both announced over the weekend that they would not be seeking the seat.
Ager campaign responds
Jamie Ager’s campaign doesn’t see Balkcom as any different from Edwards. Grayson Barnette, Ager’s campaign manager, said this vacancy is just another in a string of issues for the NC-11 seat.
“There’s no difference between Jennifer Balkcom and Chuck Edwards,” he said. “Jennifer Balkcom is going to do the exact same thing as Chuck Edwards, which is to drop the ball and not deliver Helene recovery results.”
While the 11th District is in a largely conservative region of North Carolina, it includes liberal Buncombe County and other small urban pockets. Most of the district was badly devastated by Helene two years ago.

sources.news_title: GOP executive team chooses a replacement for NC’s Chuck Edwards on ballot
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — Republicans in Western North Carolina have a new candidate running to represent them in Congress.
The 11th Congressional District Republican Party Executive Committee chose state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, a Republican from Hendersonville, to replace Rep. Chuck Edwards on the ballot.
“I’m grateful for the outpouring of support I’ve received to pursue the Republican nomination for North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District,” Balkcom said prior to the decision.
Last week, the House Committee on Ethics found substantial evidence that Edwards, 65, of Flat Rock, sexually harassed two young female staffers around 40 years his junior, and created a hostile work environment.
Edwards denies any wrongdoing. His consultant said the ethics committee’s report exonerated him because it didn’t find evidence that he had sex with staffers, propositioned them or broke the law.
However, after pressure from Republicans including House Speaker Mike Johnson and Sen. Ted Budd, Edwards announced around 3:30 a.m. Tuesday he would drop his reelection campaign.
That left the 61 members of Western North Carolina’s Republican Party executive committee choosing a new nominee to run in the general election.
Who is Jennifer Balkcom?
Balkcom, who is in her mid-40s, is in her second term in the state House after succeeding Tim Moffitt, who moved to the Senate in 2023 to succeed Edwards when he moved to Congress.
Balkcom, who works in banking, ran in 2022 on preserving North Carolina’s farmland.
In the House, Balkcom supported legislation known as the Parents’ Bill of Rights and the Parents’ Medical Bill of Rights, as well as school vouchers, gun rights, deportation of criminal immigrants in the country without permission and banning transgender individuals from women’s sports. She also wants to eliminate the state income tax.
She opposes abortion, gun control and teaching about race in schools.
Balkcom was born and raised in Henderson County, growing up on her family farm. She graduated from East Henderson High School and Blue Ridge Community College.
She served on boards and clubs including the Hendersonville Women’s Club, the Henderson County Education Foundation, the county planning board, and boards for Advent Health Foundation and the St. Gerard House, a nonprofit that helps people with autism.
She and her husband, Clint, have one son together.
How did we get here?
Edwards withdrew his name, in writing, at 4 p.m. Aug. 3.
Many notable names were thrown out as potential successors. But as the week went on, each announced they wouldn’t seek Edwards’ seat. That included state lawmakers like Sens. Kevin Corbin and Tim Moffitt and Rep. Jake Johnson.
Moffitt was considered the frontrunner until he pulled his name out of consideration over the weekend.
When that happened, Balkcom, who had endorsed Moffitt for the job, put her name up for consideration. And she received support from prominent Republicans, including House Speaker Destin Hall and Rep. Tricia Cotham.
When Balkcom entered the race she said, “I hadn’t planned to go to Washington. But I’ve learned without my life that when your community needs you, you don’t sit on the sidelines; you step up.”
Other names considered included Matthew Burril, Ken McKim, Chad Nesbitt and Kristie Sluder.
Burril previously ran in the U.S. House district, while McKim and Sluder both ran for the state Senate seat. Nesbitt runs a local news site.
North Carolina law allows anyone in the state to run for a congressional seat, regardless of where they live.
State law gives power to the executive committee to choose who replaces a nominee on the ballot if the nominee withdraws.
State of the race
Now, Balkcom must face off against the Democratic nominee, Jamie Ager.
Ager is a fourth-generation farmer and owner of Hickory Nut Gap Farms. His brother, father and grandfather have all held political office.
Ager has more than $2 millio n in his war chest.
Balkcom has 84 days to start campaigning and raising money ahead of the Nov. 3 election.

A panel of Republican officials in North Carolina selected a state lawmaker Monday as the GOP nominee in a House race after embattled Rep. Chuck Edwards dropped his re-election bid following sexual harassment allegations.
Jennifer Balkcom, who represents a state legislative district in Henderson County, will face Jamie Ager, who won the Democratic primary in March.
The North Carolina GOP’s Executive Committee for the 11th Congressional District picked Balkcom to replace Edwards in compliance with state law given how late in the campaign he dropped out.
Balkcom faces a sprint to Election Day, which is less than three months away. Absentee ballots are set to start going out Sept. 4, giving her just a few weeks to make her case to some voters.
She announced her intention to seek the nomination less than 24 hours ago.
“This race is too important to sit out,” Balkcom wrote in a statement Sunday on X, adding that Western North Carolina “needs a strong voice right now” as it continues to rebuild after Hurricane Helene.
Balkcom’s candidacy was heavily boosted by power players in the state. North Carolina House Speaker Destin Hall, a Republican, endorsed her on social media Monday afternoon, calling her “the right person at the right time.”
“Jennifer is a principled conservative, a tireless advocate for her district, and a leader who gets things done,” Hall wrote on X.
The state GOP’s executive director, Zachary Almond, congratulated Balkcom on X after her nomination was announced, saying he was “excited to work alongside her and her team throughout the election cycle.”
Edwards, who had been endorsed by President Donald Trump, announced last week that he would serve out his term in Congress but would not seek a third term in the House. His decision came days after the House Ethics Committee recommended a censure following a probe that found “substantial reason to believe Representative Edwards violated House Rules related to sexual harassment and hostile workplaces.”
He has repeatedly denied wrongdoing, and the Ethics Committee said Edwards, who cooperated with the panel’s investigation, had denied that any of his actions were meant to be sexual or romantic in nature. Attorneys for Edwards wrote a 15-page response to the committee’s findings, calling them “unfounded.”
Edwards previously called the allegations “baseless,” and in May he said he welcomed an investigation.
Edwards was elected to the House in 2022 after having ousted the scandal-ridden Rep. Madison Cawthorn in the GOP primary. Before that, the district was represented by Mark Meadows, who led the House Freedom Caucus before he stepped down to become White House chief of staff during Trump’s first term.
Edwards won his seat by more than 13 percentage points in 2024, but Democrats are hopeful they can flip it as Republicans seek to defend their narrow majority in the House heading into the midterm elections.

sources.news_title: Balkcom chosen to replace Edwards as GOP nominee in 11th District
sources.text:
The North Carolina Republican Party selected state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to replace U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards as the Republican nominee for the 11th Congressional District on Monday, the party said.
Balkcom has represented the 117th district in North Carolina since 2023.
“Western North Carolina is where I was born, raised, and chose to raise my own family,” Balkcom said. “It has been an incredible honor to fight for Henderson County in Raleigh, and I will take that fight to Washington and work every single day to make life more affordable for working families, improve community safety, support our farmers, and ensure we have the resources we need to continue to recover from Hurricane Helene.”
Members of the N.C. GOP offered their support for Balkcom after the announcement.
“She is committed to fighting for our families, defending our conservative values, and making sure Western North Carolina has a strong advocate in Congress,” Jason Simmons, Chairman of the North Carolina Republican Party, said.
The 2022 election saw Rep. Balkcom win a competitive three-way Republican primary. After that, she won the general election and represented N.C.’s House of Representatives’ 117th District.
Edwards ended his reelection campaign on August 5 after the House Ethics Committee recommended he be censured for unprofessional and inappropriate behavior toward two female aides in his office.

sources.news_title: Chuck Edwards' potential replacements after he dropped re-election bid
sources.text:
Congressman Chuck Edwards has dropped out of his bid for re-election, leaving his party with the task of selecting a replacement to take on Democrats in what appears to be an increasingly tough contest for the GOP.
The North Carolina Republican made the decision after the House Ethics Committee recommended he be censured for inappropriate conduct toward female staffers. The committee found no evidence Edwards engaged in sexual activity with the woman or explicitly propositioned any employee, though its investigation detailed inappropriate comments and expensive gifts, including jewelry, designer purses, guns and vacations.
Edwards has denied wrongdoing and will serve out the remainder of his term, set to end on January 3.
“After much prayer and reflection, I’ve decided to withdraw from my re-election campaign,” Edwards posted to X. “I will complete my current term. Serving Western North Carolina has been the honor of my life.”
Who Are Edwards’ Potential Replacements?
According to local reports, five names have emerged as possible replacements for Edwards, one of whom will take on Democrat Jamie Ager come November.
Jennifer Balkcom
Jennifer Balkcom is a member of the North Carolina House of Representatives and has held her District 117 seat since early 2023. She announced on Sunday that she would be entering the race.
“This race is too important to sit out,” she wrote on X. “We must hold this seat, preserve our mountain values, work with President Trump’s administration to continue rebuilding Western North Carolina, and make sure Washington never forgets the people who call these mountains home.”
Ken McKim
Ken McKim is a prolific figure in North Carolina Republican politics, having run for the state senate in 2006 and launched a congressional bid in 2021, according to ABC13 News.
In a 2021 profile in Hendersonville Lightning, McKim described his platform as one of “true conservatism, seeing that our nation’s founding documents and laws are adhered to, protecting individual liberties, controlling government spending and lowering taxes.”
Matthew Burril
Matthew Burril is an investment manager and financial professional, whose experience also includes an unsuccessful run for North Carolina’s 11th congressional district in 2022.
Kristie Sluder
Kristie Sluder ran for election to the North Carolina State Senate in 2024, but was defeated by the Democratic candidate, Julie Mayfield, who secured 69 percent of the vote per Ballotpedia.
Her campaign website listed increasing the supply of affordable housing, protecting “individual rights” and “rebuild[ing] the nuclear family” among her key aims.
Chad Nesbitt
Chad Nesbitt is a businessman, independent journalist and founder of Skyline News, an Asheville-based media company.
Nesbitt announced his intention to run in a video posted to Facebook, and said he was "asked by three committee members" whether he would consider running to replace Edwards on the ballot.
Newsweek has attempted to contact the candidates via past campaign emails, current business emails or social media accounts.
Who is Favored in the Race?
On Monday, the North Carolina Republican party will host a meeting to discuss Edwards’ replacement—a decision that will be made by the party’s executive committee for North Carolina's 11th Congressional District.
Nominations will be made during Monday evening’s meeting, and candidates must secure over 50 percent of the vote to avoid a runoff with the two most popular candidates.
President Donald Trump carried Edwards’ district—NC-11—by 10 points in 2024 and has not elected a Democrat since 2010, but polls suggest that Republicans could struggle to retain the House seat.
Probabilistic forecasting from VoteHub.com has Ager “narrowly favored” over the eventual nominee with a 62 percent chance of victory and an estimated vote share of 51 percent as of Monday afternoon.
Bettors on Polymarket, meanwhile, give the Democrats a 57 percent chance of victory—odds that shot up to 66 percent following the ethics committee investigation and remain higher than before Edwards’ withdrawal.
And some experts consider the seat a bellwether of how competitive this year’s midterms prove to be.
“Democrats do not need to win NC-11 to have a successful midterm and take over the U.S. House of Representatives,” Christopher Cooper, a professor of political science and public affairs at Western Carolina University, wrote in June. “But if they are competitive there, or if Ager actually flips the seat, it will likely mean that the national environment has moved well beyond an ordinary midterm and into wave territory.”

sources.news_title: North Carolina GOP picks Balkcom to replace Edwards as congressional nominee
sources.text:
North Carolina Republicans on Monday picked a state legislator to be the GOP nominee in the state’s 11th Congressional District, replacing an incumbent who ended his reelection plans last week.
Party officials in the district picked State Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, R-Henderson, to replace U.S. Rep. Chuck Edwards on the ballot. Edwards, who has represented the district since 2023, dropped out of the race on Wednesday after a U.S. House committee announced plans to sanction him following an investigation into allegations of sexual harassment.
Other WRAL Top Stories
Balkcom now faces Democrat Jamie Ager in a race that political analysts say was tightening prior to the committee’s findings.
Voters in the district supported President Donald Trump over Democrat Kamala Harris by 9.5 percentage points in the 2024 election. However, Ager outraised Edwards by a nearly 9-to-1 margin last quarter. And Ager, who owns a farm and a meat business, has built support by advocating for more federal aid for victims of Hurricane Helene, which ravaged the district in September 2024.
The Cook Political Report, a Virginia-based nonpartisan group that studies the competitiveness of elections, in June changed its rating of the race to “Lean Republican,” which means the race has become competitive but that the GOP nominee maintains an advantage. Cook previously rated the race “Likely Republican,” which means a race isn’t considered competitive but has the potential to be under certain circumstances.
Balkcom, a mortgage loan officer, has risen through the House Republican ranks quickly since winning her seat in 2022. She chairs the House Insurance Committee, as well as the House Appropriations on Agriculture and Natural and Economic Resources Committee.
In her first term, Balkcom was a primary sponsor of legislation that banned transgender girls and women from competing in women's sports in middle school, high school and college athletics in North Carolina. Republican legislators in 2023 voted to override a veto by then-Gov. Roy Cooper to enact the bill into law.
This year, Balkcom led an effort to prevent foreign countries from buying certain land in North Carolina. House Bill 133, which Democratic Gov. Josh Stein signed last month, bans people or companies affiliated with foreign adversaries of the U.S. from buying land within 50 miles of a military installation — and from buying any farmland anywhere in the state.
Balkcom announced her campaign to replace Edwards less than 24 hours before GOP officials in his district met Monday evening to discuss a new Republican nominee.
Balkcom said in a 10:21 p.m. social media post on Sunday that she hadn’t planned on seeking a U.S. House seat but had been encouraged to run and felt compelled to “step up.” At least two other legislators from western North Carolina — state Sens. Kevin Corbin and Tim Moffitt — had announced that they were considering a run for the nomination but ultimately decided against it.
Party officials in Balkcom’s district must now nominate a new candidate to backfill the position in the legislature. All legislative seats are up for election in November. Balkcom faced Democrat Lynne Russo in the state’s 117th House District, which leans Republican.

sources.news_title: Balkcom in, Moffitt out, in NC-11 replacement talks
sources.text:
Monday evening, Republicans in western North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District will be meeting to decide their GOP candidate to replace, Congressman Chuck Edwards, R-NC11, after a House Ethics Committee report detailed violations of House rules related to sexual harassment and creating a hostile workplace.
Under North Carolina law, when a candidate withdraws this close to the election, the political party in this case, the Republican Party, selects a replacement nominee. North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District is made up of 16 counties: Avery, Buncombe, Cherokee, Clay, Graham, Haywood, Henderson, Jackson, Macon, Madison, McDowell, Mitchell, Polk, Swain, Transylvania, and Yancey.
CANDIDATES
Late last week, State Sen. Tim Moffitt, R-Henderson, appeared to be frontrunner in the replacement contest; however, over the weekend Moffitt said he would not be placing his name in the running.
“After careful consideration, I have decided not to seek the Republican nomination for North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District,” Moffitt wrote on social media. “My responsibilities to my family and businesses would not allow me to commit to more than a few years in Congress. Western North Carolina deserves a representative who can give the full measure of time required, both day-to-day and over the long-term. Anything less would be unfair to the people of this district.”
He continued by thanking everyone for their support and encouragement during the process.
Adam Smith, who challenged Edwards in the March primary and previously said “nothing is off the table,” has also announced that he will not seek the nomination.
“I have decided not to seek the nomination,” Smith wrote. “I want to be direct about my reasons. I have never run from a fight in my life, not overseas and not at home, and I know what it takes to win a battle in 87 days: infrastructure already built and the full weight of the party committed from day one. The stakes are too high for anything less. This seat must stay in conservative hands, and the best way I can serve that mission right now is to help our party unite immediately behind its nominee instead of dividing it on the eve of battle.”
Rep. Jennifer Balkcom, R-Henderson, has announced she will be seeking the nomination and is viewed as the current favorite. The two term House member, said it’s time to step up.
“I hadn’t planned to go to Washington,” wrote Balkcom, “But I’ve learned throughout my life that when your community needs you, you don’t sit on the sidelines; you step up. Western North Carolina needs a strong voice right now. Our communities are still rebuilding from Hurricane Helene. Our farmers, families, and small businesses need someone who understands them. And too often, Washington simply doesn’t understand the people, values, and challenges of our mountains.”
Balkcom said her decision to enter the race was driven by a desire to fight for Western North Carolina and ensure the region has a strong voice in Washington.
“So, after much prayer, reflection, and conversations with my family, I’m in,” Balkcom said. “I will seek the Republican nomination for North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District. This race is too important to sit out. We must hold this seat, preserve our mountain values, work with President Trump’s Administration to continue rebuilding Western North Carolina, and make sure Washington never forgets the people who call these mountains home.”

5 potential candidates considered to replace Chuck Edwards as NC-11 GOP nominee
ASHEVILLE, N.C. (WLOS) — Five potential candidates are being considered to replace Congressman Chuck Edwards as the Republican nominee for North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District ahead of a committee meeting on Monday, Aug. 10.
The North Carolina Republican Party's 11th Congressional District Executive Committee will choose between:
- Jennifer Balkcom, a Republican member of the North Carolina House of Representatives.
- Ken McKim, a Republican political figure who notably ran as a candidate for the North Carolina State Senate in 2006 and briefly filed as a congressional candidate in 2021–2022.
- Chad Nesbitt, a Republican activist and president of Skyline News in Asheville.
- Matthew Burril, a Republican who ran for the U.S. House to represent North Carolina's 11th Congressional District. He lost in the Republican primary on May 17, 2022.
- Kristie Sluder, a Republican who ran for election to the North Carolina State Senate to represent District 49. She lost in the general election on November 5, 2024.
The person selected will take Edwards’ place on the Republican ticket for November’s midterm election.
SEN. TIM MOFFITT SAYS HE WON’T RUN FOR GOP NOMINATION IN NC’S 11TH DISTRICT
The list of potential candidates comes after state Sen. Tim Moffitt announced he would not seek the nomination. Moffitt had been viewed as a potential frontrunner for the seat.
“It is surprising,” said Chris Cooper, director of Western Carolina University’s Public Policy Institute. “This is obviously moving very, very quickly, but I think a lot of folks, myself included, thought that Tim Moffitt was probably the leading candidate.”
Moffitt announced his decision on X, writing that his responsibilities to his family and businesses would not allow him to commit to more than a few years in Congress.
READ MORE: HOW REPUBLICANS WILL CHOOSE REP. CHUCK EDWARDS' REPLACEMENT FOR NC-11 RACE
NCGOP executive director Zach Almond told News 13 he is confident the committee will reach a decision Monday night.
“I think that coming out of tomorrow night, they'll select someone who will do really well in the November election,” Almond said.
The meeting is scheduled to begin at 6:30 p.m. Monday.
“Really, it could be anybody,” Cooper said. “Let’s remember, this is not like a normal election. State law says the executive committee gets to make this decision.”

sources.news_title: Balkcom gains NC-11 GOP nomination
sources.text:
Current State Rep. Jennifer Balkcom will replace Chuck Edwards as the Republican on the ballot for North Carolina’s 11th Congressional District seat.
Balkcom was nominated by the district GOP executive committee the evening of Aug. 10 at Buncombe County’s party headquarters.
The process began with early morning tweet on Aug. 5, wherein Edwards announced he would no longer seek a third congressional term. The withdrawal came on the heels of a damning House Ethics Committee report that detailed a pattern of harassment by Edwards toward a pair of young female staffers.
Balkcom is a Henderson County small business owner who’s served two terms in the North Carolina House. Although she was running for a third, she will have to leave that campaign to appear on the ballot for NC-11.
From the time Edwards said he wouldn’t seek reelection, the list of potential replacements ebbed and flowed as rumors spread and were just as quickly squelched. The day of the announcement, Sen. Kevin Corbin expressed interest in the position but within hours said he was out. Sen. Tim Moffitt emerged as an early favorite but bowed out on Aug. 8.
The day of Edwards’ announcement, while some Republicans initially expressed interest in Balkcom running, she said she’d refrain and would instead support Moffitt. That day, both Adam Smith and Christian Reagan told SMN that they would run. Smith later withdrew, and Reagan continued to seek the nomination. On Aug. 8, a candidate list obtained by The Smoky Mountain News indicated that the candidates were Moffitt, Sherry Higgins, Chad Nesbitt, Ken McKim and Kristie Sluder.
Around that time, the talk around the district was that state Rep. Karl Gillespie, of Macon County, was throwing his hat in the ring, but the afternoon of Aug. 9, he told party leaders that wouldn’t be the case. When a new list of candidates obtained by SMN was released a bit later, it included Sluder, McKim, Nesbitt and newcomer Matthew Burril. It also included Balkcom.
Now that Balkcom has secured the nomination, she will face off against Democrat Jamie Ager in what may become one of the higher-profile congressional races in the country.
Check back with The Smoky Mountain News tomorrow for a full story.
